item.title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches (146 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/were-asking-appeals-court-require-warrant-alpr-searches, See on Hacker News

Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.

But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin, ALPRs give law enforcement “a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.

We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.

Related Updates

We Demand More Information on How Marin Cops Illegally Shared Flock ALPR Data

The Marin County Sheriff’s Office is the latest California law enforcement agency to get caught sharing automated license plate reader (ALPR) data from their Flock Safety system with out-of-state and federal agencies. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California are calling them out for this direct violation of California law,...

The High Crime of “LMAO”: How Cops Are Treating Flock's Mass Surveillance As a Joke

With no warrant requirements, limited guardrails, and deficient audit processes, ALPR databases have fostered a culture of unrestricted access to everyone’s location information. This culture of abuse has allowed police to treat a mass surveillance network like their own personal search engine, permitting the tracking of the movements of everyday...

Texas and Florida Step Back from ALPRs

Within the last few days, two important state actions have dealt a big blow to automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks. This is just the latest proof of the growing tide of public opposition to mass surveillance. After years of successful grassroots battles to pull these cameras from local streets...

item.title: LinkedIn, Monster take down over 1000 fake job postings after CBC investigation (233 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/linkedin-monster-take-down-over-1-000-fake-job-postings-after-cbc-investigation-9.7415379, See on Hacker News

More than 1,500 misleading job postings — offering remote work, no experience needed — have been taken down from LinkedIn and Monster after a CBC visual investigation revealed the listings funnelled unsuspecting applicants to a multi-level marketing (MLM) company that asked for money.

CBC connected a network of travel-related pages posting suspicious jobs — positions like "Work From Home Travel Planner and Virtual Customer Support Representative" — to a U.S.-based MLM called Evolution Travel. Some of the roles promised to pay up to $75,000 US per year.

In reality, there was no job and no salary.

Applicants were quickly directed to join virtual information sessions, where they were asked to pay hundreds of dollars up front, followed by a monthly subscription fee. The program promised to teach members how to make money from booking travel as an independent agent and recruiting others into the program, taking a cut of their commissions.

WATCH | Investigating who's behind hundreds of fake job postings:

Exposing who’s behind fake job ads online

Major job-seeking platforms host hundreds of listings for remote travel jobs that promise salaries up to $75,000 with no experience required. CBC Visual Investigations applied online and found that there is no job: The ads lead to a U.S.-based multi-level marketing scheme that asks unsuspecting applicants to pay up front. After flagging the listings to LinkedIn and Monster, nearly 1,500 were taken offline.

The companies went by names like Wanderwell Collective, Professional Travel Hub, Remote-Careers, Sky Land & Ocean Travel and Sunkissed Getaways.

The job postings made no mention of Evolution Travel or sign-up fees.

Many of the jobs did not require experience and promised to pay up to $75,000 US. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC; LinkedIn)

"This is disgusting," said Jay Jones, a Chicago-based job listing investigator who CBC shared its findings with. "They catch you with the lure of the fake job. The money is great, [successful applicants] get to stay at home. You have to pay to get work — that's not how work works."

Misleading job postings — including ones that require payment or lead to MLMs — are strictly prohibited on platforms like LinkedIn and other job sites.

Jay Jones investigates misleading and fake jobs online. (CBC)

"It feels in so many ways that we're living in a funhouse mirror," said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think-tank that focuses on economic resilience and digital sovereignty.

These postings risk "eroding confidence — confidence in the self and confidence that there is, frankly, meaningful work out there for people that is worth pursuing."

Jobs were 'misleading': LinkedIn

MLMs are not illegal in Canada or the U.S. However, in the U.S., companies and individuals could face fines if they are found to violate the U.S. Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits "unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce."

"I would consider [these job posts] misleading… and would invite enforcement by either the FTC, the state governments or other federal enforcement agencies," said William Kovacic, former FTC chairman and commissioner, with whom CBC also shared its findings.

One independent agent behind multiple travel businesses linked to misleading jobs ads CBC identified — Wanderwell Collective, Destination Knot, Aisle and Abroad, and Professional Travel Hub — was Diedre Norton. In one video posted to YouTube, Norton said she had a network of 300 recruits for Evolution Travel.

Even though Evolution Travel’s founder, David McCovy, praised her in online videos as being a top performer, Norton denied being affiliated with the program before hanging up on CBC News.

Screenshot of an online video showing Evolution founder David McCovy during a conference. (EvolutionTravelCafe/YouTube)

McCovy did not respond to CBC’s requests for comment.

A representative from Evolution Travel who only identified themselves by their title, chief operating officer, told CBC they have consistently told their independent agents not to post job ads on any platforms.

Late last month, LinkedIn took down close to 900 ads connected to Evolution Travel, saying it had removed them because they were "misleading and violated" company policy, adding "the companies behind them will no longer be able to post jobs" on the platform.

Monster took down 600 listings, saying it has "clear policies prohibiting misleading job postings and multi-level marketing opportunities, and we take action to remove listings that do not meet our standards."

Hundreds of job postings posted to LinkedIn and Monster actually brought applicants into the recruiting process for a multi-level marketing company, a CBC News visual investigation has found. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, LinkedIn, Monster)

Detecting fake jobs

Evolution Travel does not operate in Canada, but CBC journalists still came across the job posting in their feeds. They were also recommended in emails from LinkedIn.

The ads contained immediate red flags. The travel companies named in the ads had minimal to no presence online, and there were close to 1,500 postings, often with almost identical job descriptions.

Many of the jobs did not require experience and were remote. CBC found more than 1,500 misleading or fake jobs. (LinkedIn)

The jobs, in many cases, required no education, no prior experience and often did not require a resumé.

CBC applied for eight jobs on LinkedIn and Monster, attaching a blank document as a resumé in cases that required it. Upon applying, the team was sent automated emails to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel. 

CBC journalists were sent automated emails and asked to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel upon applying for the jobs. (CBC)

Evolution Travel and its partner Archer Travel Services describe themselves as an international "home-based travel business" that trains its members to book travel and earn a commission.

But it's not just about booking travel. Archer Travel’s website describes Evolution Travel as its "recruiting partner" and describes it as a "network marketing" company — another term for multi-level marketing, according to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

A compensation plan for members on Evolution Travel’s website shows a percentage of commissions and monthly bonuses are paid to the most effective recruiters, with membership tiers up to "8 Star Platinum" for recruiting 100,000 people.

Documents show compensation plans for Evolution Travel. (Evolution Travel)

None of this was mentioned in the information sessions CBC attended, which covered travel booking exclusively. When a CBC journalist posing as a job applicant asked about getting commissions from their own recruits, the session host said it was not covered in the information sessions and that the person who invited them into the program would address it.

Session hosts also didn’t disclose there is a hidden $50 annual fee in the independent contractor agreement, seen by CBC, when signing up.

A screenshot from an Evolution virtual session shows the packages attendees can pay to enrol in the program. (Evolution Travel)

Former FTC chairman and commissioner Kovacic said if he were still at the agency, he would be looking into the company.

"[Fees are] not presented in the initial interaction," he said. "It's shrouded in a way that's very important and would mislead users."

27,000 independent contractors

Job seekers have been complaining about Evolution Travel, its members and agents like Deidre Norton online and to the Better Business Bureau for years.

In 2021, Evolution Travel was among 1,000 companies put on notice by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission that they could face fines if they or their representatives made "misleading, or deceptive representations" about a "money-making opportunity." 

Kovacic said a firm that "defied" FTC notices and continued to persist in these practices would be a "worthy target for an investigation."

CBC News found numerous complaints online about companies linked to the job postings. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, Reddit, Better Business Bureau)

Ron Archer, the CEO of Archer Travel Services, said that the company does "not condone illegal job postings and addresses them when we are made aware."

Yet in videos online, travel agents connected to Evolution Travel talked openly about using LinkedIn job postings to recruit people into the business.

Archer said they cannot "tell people how they train for their business" because they have "27,000 independent contractors around the world."

"LinkedIn is a big one," said one member in a June 2026 training video posted to YouTube. "We have quite a few different trainings on how to post on LinkedIn."

Jay Jones, who has gotten tens of thousands of jobs taken down from platforms himself, said companies like LinkedIn and Monster generate revenue through this traffic.

"There's no actual vetting of what companies get to be created, what jobs get to be listed," said Jones. "People coming [to LinkedIn] believing that there are real opportunities are greeted with this MLM nonsense."

For any tips related to this investigation, contact eric.szeto@cbc.ca or the visual investigation team’s inbox: vi@cbc.ca

item.title: US IRS free online tax filing open source repo (2025) (158 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/IRS-Public/direct-file, See on Hacker News

Direct File is a service from the United States Government that provides taxpayers the option to electronically file their federal tax return for free, directly with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Direct File is an interview-based service that is intended to work as well on a mobile phone as it does on a laptop, tablet, or desktop computer. It is available in English and Spanish and is designed to be accessible to taxpayers who have a variety of attitudes, aptitudes, abilities, and access needs.

Direct File interprets the United States' Internal Revenue Code (26 USC) as plain language questions, the answers to which should be known to taxpayers without need of external instructions or publications. Taxpayers' answers are then translated into standard tax forms and transmitted to the IRS's Modernized e-File (MeF) API, which is available for authorized public use. These questions and logic, developed in close collaboration with the IRS Office of Chief Counsel, as well as the associated test cases and scenarios, may be useful for others working on products that need to accurately interpret United States tax law as of Tax Year 2024.

Direct File also incorporates the Fact Graph, a declarative, XML-based knowledge graph data structure that is designed to reason about incomplete information, such as a partially completed tax return. The Fact Graph is written in the Scala programming language; it runs on the JVM on the backend and is transpiled via Scala.js to run on the client as well. Direct File's Fact Graph is not domain-specific, and it may be useful to revenue agencies and as a reference for business rules engine implementations.

Although Direct File only files federal tax returns, United States taxpayers also have state and local filing obligations. Direct File facilitates the completion of these obligations by enabling taxpayers to optionally import their federal return data into a third-party tool that can file state and/or local taxes, without needing to reenter information. This transaction is enabled via a State API, which transfers both standard MeF XML as well as an enriched JSON format that includes additional data elements that were identified as being useful to state revenue agencies to streamline the state tax experience.

Direct File was developed by an in-house team of technologists at the IRS. The blended, cross-agency team included support from USDS and GSA, as well as vendor teams TrussWorks, Coforma, and ATI.

For a more details on the program and its history see https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p5969.pdf and https://www.irs.gov/filing/irs-direct-file-for-free

This repository has been archived and is no longer maintained. The code is provided for historical reference and may contain unpatched or unknown vulnerabilities. It should not be used in production systems.

Where do I start?

See ONBOARDING.md if you want to jump into running Direct File locally

Exempted Code

Not all source code, documentation and metadata used in the development of Direct File is included in this repository. Specifically, any code or data that is considered Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Federal Tax Information (FTI), Sensitive But Unclassified (SBU), or source code developed for National Security Systems (NSS), as defined in 40 U.S.C. § 11103, is exempt. Due to these restrictions, certain pieces of functionality have been removed or rewritten.

Authorities

Legal foundations for work include:

  • Source code Harmonization And Reuse in Information Technology Act" of 2024, Public Law 118 - 187
  • OMB Memorandum M-16-21, “Federal Source Code Policy: Achieving Efficiency, Transparency, and Innovation through Reusable and Open Source Software,” August 8, 2016
  • Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Part 27 – Patents, Data, and Copyrights
  • Digital Government Strategy: “Digital Government: Building a 21st Century Platform to Better Serve the American People,” May 23, 2012
  • Federal Information Technology Acquisition Reform Act (FITARA), December 2014 (National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2015, Title VIII, Subtitle D)
  • E-Government Act of 2002, Public Law 107-347
  • Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, Public Law 104-106

item.title: A Family Tree of Software Job Titles (257 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://zwischenzugs.com/2026/11/03/a-family-tree-of-software-job-titles/, See on Hacker News

For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’. Before I got that job title I’d done much the same work under other names, and since then I’ve watched the same work get called SRE, and then it seemed to morph towards platform engineering. If you’ve been in this industry for any length of time you’ll have seen titles come and go like this, and you might have wondered where they all came from.

So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now.

It’s here: ianmiell.github.io/sw-job-title-family-tree

What It Is

There are 104 titles, from ‘Computer’ (a person, not a machine) at the top to ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ at the bottom.

Time runs from top to bottom, in five-year rows. The titles sit in seven coloured columns by family:

  • Development
  • Analysis, architecture and leadership
  • Operations and infrastructure
  • Networks and security
  • Data and AI
  • Quality and test
  • Support and customer-facing

A solid arrow means the title grew out of its parent. A dashed arrow means influence, or a common career move. Landmark titles are in bold.

On the site you can click a family to see just that column (here’s Data & AI), or click a title to get its history, background and connections (here’s SRE).

The whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions. Each title is one line in the .dot file, and the picture is rendered with:

$ dot -Tsvg job_title_family_tree.dot -o job_title_family_tree.svg

Adding a title is three small edits: a node in its family’s column, an entry in the row for its five-year period, and its parent arrows.

A word on the dates. They’re roughly when a title became common, not its first recorded use, and they’re my best estimates, not sourced citations. Some are well known (SRE at Google in 2003, ‘DevOps’ coined in 2009, ‘Data Scientist’ in 2008). Plenty are a ‘c.’ and a shrug.

Six Things I Noticed

Drawing it out made a few patterns hard to miss.

1) Coding Started Out as the Clerical Bit

In 1947, Goldstine and von Neumann’s ‘Planning and Coding of Problems’ split the work of using a computer in two: mathematicians planned the problem, and coders translated the plan into machine instructions. Coding was treated as lower-status clerical work, and much of it was done by women.

It turned out that coding eventually became the hard, creative part, and the coder merged into the programmer.

Go back further and it’s stranger still. Several of the first ENIAC programmers were recruited from the Army’s human computers, people whose job was to compute by hand. So the job gave its name to the machine, and its people to programming.

2) Titles Break Apart, Then Join Back Up

The webmaster turned up around 1993, and was often a single person who wrote the HTML, ran the webserver (often a box under a desk), answered the email, and kept the site up (sometimes by kicking it, more often by plugging it back in after kicking it).

By the mid-2000s the title had all but gone, as it was unfashionably ancient. The code went to web developers, the servers to sysadmins, and the content to editors and designers.

Then the web developer split into front-end and back-end around 2005, and the two joined back up again as ‘full-stack’ around 2008.

This is the centralisation/distribution see-saw I’ve written about before, playing out in job titles.

3) Some Titles Don’t Last

The prompt engineer made headlines in 2023 with a few eye-wateringly well-paid job listings. As the models got better, the skill became part of other jobs, and on the tree it gets absorbed into the AI engineer almost as soon as it appears.

The scrum master is a slower version of the same story: demand peaked in the 2010s, and many organisations have since folded it back into engineering management or delivery roles.

The newest title on the tree is the ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ (c. 2025). The description for it currently says “time will tell whether it stays a separate title”. I’m not taking bets.

4) Names Get Recycled

‘Systems Engineer’ is two different jobs on the tree. At IBM in the 1960s it was a pre-sales role, working with customers to design installations and get them running. In the 1990s, thanks largely to Microsoft’s MCSE certification, it meant a more senior, design-oriented sysadmin. Same title, different branch, no relation.

‘Configuration management’ started as a 1960s US defence discipline for tracking hardware changes, became software version control in the 1970s, and then came back decades later as the name for tools like Puppet and Chef.

5) The New Thing Is Often an Old Thing

The ‘forward deployed engineer’ (FDE) is one of the hottest titles of 2025, as OpenAI, Anthropic and plenty of AI startups hire FDEs to get AI working inside their customers’ organisations.

Palantir built its business around them from about 2010: software engineers embedded with a customer, often on site, building whatever is needed to make the product work for that customer’s problem.

Which sounds a lot like IBM’s systems engineers of the 1960s, who worked with customers before and after the sale, designing installations and getting systems running. (It also sounds a lot like old-style consulting, but I would say that.)

6) The DevOps Debate Is There

Ben Treynor Sloss defined SRE as “what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team”. DevOps was meant as a culture of developers and operations working together, but by about 2011 ‘DevOps Engineer’ had become a job title, usually for whoever did the automation. On the tree, the arrow between SRE and DevOps points both ways. Platform engineering has both of them as parents, and was sold around 2022 as ‘the successor to DevOps’.

The Dev/Ops divide has never been resolved. It just keeps getting new names.

Why Bother?

When I’m asked what the difference is between a DevOps engineer, an SRE and a platform engineer, the honest answer is always a little history lesson. This is the shortest version of that lesson I’ve managed so far.

The dates are best guesses, and I’ll have missed titles, mangled some lineages and drawn arrows people will argue with. If you know better, let me know, or raise a PR on the repo.

Which brings me back to the coders.

In 1947 coding was the clerical bit, and the real work was in the planning. Wind forward eighty years and you’ll hear much the same said about coding again, because AI. Last time, the coders turned out to be doing the hard part.

I’ll leave you to draw that arrow yourself.

item.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages (728 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.crissyfield.de/research/lovable-en/, See on Hacker News

Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive Data

AI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.

Diesen Artikel auf Deutsch lesen

About Lovable

Lovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to people with little or no programming experience.

Lovable grew out of Osika’s open-source project “GPT Engineer”, released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.

Visit the Lovable website

The Promise

Lovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: Is that data protected against unauthorized access?

In its marketing, Lovable repeatedly emphasizes that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects. This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable’s Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.

That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.

Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German).

Research Question

We wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.

The result: We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.

Methodology

We focused on the database service Supabase. Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable’s own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.

Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl, we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.

24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites (30%).

Limitations

Email addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.

We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.

Data Leaks

We found many serious cases of exposed data, including:

  • A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. More than 200,000 chat messages were also accessible.

  • Several event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales, with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.

  • A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.

  • In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed more than 1,000 records containing identity document details, including passport numbers, expiration dates, and nationalities. These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.

  • Other accessible content included tens of thousands of contracts, invoices, personal photo albums, and internal WhatsApp communications.

  • We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, 280,000 emails sent to a provider’s customers were accessible.

Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.

Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.

Implications

Our analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.

Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.

An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.

Automated checks are no substitute for a professional security assessment.

Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.

item.title: Formalizing US Tax Code (Using Lean) (142 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lexifina.com/blog/formalizing-the-us-tax-code, See on Hacker News

Yesterday, we verified that known tax loopholes could be identified using a Lean search. Today, we set out to formalize the entire Internal Revenue Code to hunt for unknown loopholes (bugs).

Pointing a proof checker at statutes

Lean is a programming language whose type checker can also check mathematical proofs: if Lean accepts a proof, every step follows from the definitions, with nothing taken on trust. An earlier post discussed how far that kind of formalisation can reach in law,[1] and yesterday we used it on the retirement-account rules, where a blind search rediscovered the backdoor Roth.[2]

This work is part of global-law, a CC0 repository of versioned legislation and case law.[3] Our argument is that pointing AI and a proof checker at a versioned record of the law finds the contradictions and mechanical mistakes that people miss. In particular, we can catch mistakes in the text, and see what the rules allow, including what they allow by accident. To do so, we translated each section of the law into Lean, staying close to the statute’s own words, and tested it against the worked examples the IRS prints in its forms and instructions.

1. The tax law’s text has 138 drafting mistakes

The tax law is Title 26 of the US Code. Its official text is published as structured data by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, the office of the House of Representatives that compiles the Code.[4] We used the release current to 3 November 2026.

A parser then reads every cross-reference, including the ones written in words (“paragraph (2) of subsection (b)”, “such subparagraph”, “sections 922 through 927”), which carry no hyperlink. Lean checks each one. Does the provision it points to exist? Is it still in force? (verifiable via our versioned history) The checks run as a test suite, which fails whenever a new release adds a fault the last one did not have.

The suite reports 257 findings, each checked by an AI agent against the official text and its editorial notes: 98 intended (rules for past periods, and provisions enacted but not yet in effect), 21 false alarms in the editors’ own hyperlinks, and 138 real faults:

Each of the 138 has a certificate: a short Lean statement that carries its evidence from the official XML and proves the fault. For a dead reference, the evidence is the full list of what does exist under the cited provision. Lean re-checks all 138 in about two and a half minutes.

Our record of the US Code is a git history, one commit per public law,[5] so each fault can be traced to the law that wrote it. For Title 26 the record reaches back to the 1994 edition.

This check is cheap to repeat. Run against each new release of the Code, it flags a new mistake as soon as it appears, and names the law that caused it.

2. Rewriting the income tax as code that can be checked

Next we wrote down what the law calculates: the 2025 federal income tax for one household, meaning the numbers on Form 1040, including the changes made by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025.[6],[7] We did it in four parts:

  • Income, down to adjusted gross income (AGI). AGI is total income minus a few items, such as IRA contributions and student-loan interest. Most other tax rules depend on it.
  • Deductions: the standard deduction or itemized deductions, and the new deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest and people over 65.
  • The tax itself, including the alternative minimum tax (AMT), a second calculation that stops high earners from cutting their tax too far with deductions.
  • Credits, such as the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit (EITC), a credit for people on low and moderate wages.

We used AI to translate the statute into Lean. This is the lossy step, therefore we reinforce it with the following measures:

  • Each part is tested against figures the IRS publishes (the Tax Table, the EITC table, the worksheets and the examples in its publications), and checked against three independent tax programs on 5,000 households (section 3).
  • A second agent, which did not write that part, reviews it adversarially, looking for errors and for cheating, such as code written to pass the tests rather than to follow the statute.

What Lean ultimately adds is proofs that cover every input instead of a sample. For example, it proves that the SALT cap and the car-loan and overtime deductions never grow when income rises, at every income and for every filing status.

The comparison with other tax software helps us catch logical errors. That is how we caught two mistakes in our own model. It is also how we found bugs in the other tools that were logical rather than arithmetic: Tax-Calculator gives the EITC to separate filers without checking whether the spouses lived apart, and UsTaxes never attaches Schedule C to the 2025 return, so self-employment income disappears.

Writing the model turned up five things:

  • The published Code mixes 2025 and 2026 law. In six places the consolidated Code already shows the 2025 Act’s amendments that start in 2026. Read without the effective-date notes, it gives the wrong 2025 tax: the AMT phase-out at 50% instead of 25%, a charity floor and a cap on itemized deductions that do not yet apply.
  • The same Act rounds in opposite directions. The new tips and overtime deductions shrink by $100 for each full $1,000 of income over the limit, so one more dollar of income can cost $100 of deduction. The new car-loan deduction shrinks by $200 for each $1,000 “or portion thereof”, which rounds the other way, so it runs out $999 sooner than the round numbers suggest.
  • A married couple can deduct more state and local tax by filing separately. The deduction for state and local taxes (SALT) is capped, and the cap shrinks as income rises: by 30 cents for each dollar over $500,000 on a joint return. On a separate return, the law halves the cap after shrinking it, so it shrinks by only 15 cents a dollar. A couple earning $300,000 each can deduct up to $25,000 on two separate returns, but only $10,000 on one joint return.
  • The Tax Table is not the tax formula. Most people with taxable income under $100,000 look up their tax in the IRS Tax Table instead of working it out. The table differs from the formula in the law by between −$5 and +$6, and Lean proves that range for every income under $100,000 and every filing status.
  • One dollar can cost $8,046. Some benefits switch off at a line instead of fading out. A family with three children can lose its whole EITC, up to $8,046, because its investment income is one dollar over $11,950. The saver’s credit, a credit for retirement saving, works the same way: a couple who each put $2,000 into retirement accounts gets $2,000 at an income of $47,500, and $800 at $47,501.

3. Testing it against tax software people already use

A model is only useful if it gives the right answers. To check ours, we built 5,000 sample households and worked out each one’s 2025 tax four ways: with our model, and with three tools built by other teams, independently of each other and of us:

  • PolicyEngine-US, an open-source model that researchers and policymakers use to estimate how tax and benefit changes affect households;[8]
  • Tax-Calculator, the Policy Simulation Library’s open-source model of the federal income tax;[9]
  • UsTaxes, a free, open-source app for preparing your own tax return.[10]

Two thousand households were ordinary. The other 3,000 were deliberately awkward: couples filing separately, widows and widowers, students, people with tips or overtime, IRAs and health savings accounts, education and saver’s credits, and incomes over $1 million with large investment gains.

Our model and PolicyEngine-US agreed on every figure for 4,993 of the 5,000 households. The other seven differ by at most $11, all in the EITC: our model reads the IRS’s printed EITC table, while PolicyEngine-US uses the formula behind it.[11]

Tax-Calculator gave the EITC and the child and dependent care credit to married people filing separately without checking that the spouses lived apart, which the law requires. It also computed no AMT for one high-earning separate filer, where two other calculators computed $14,881.

UsTaxes had 14 bugs, each confirmed by recalculating an affected household. It drops self-employment income without a warning, because its 2025 return never attaches Schedule C, the form for business income. Its child-care credit never reaches the return. Its age test for the EITC always passes. And its self-employment tax counts a spouse’s wages against the cap on Social Security tax. Together, these bugs affect about one ordinary household in six.

The comparison caught two mistakes in our own model too. We had not counted self-employment profit toward the 20% deduction for small-business income. And we always took the larger of the standard and itemized deductions, although the law lets you choose to itemize a smaller amount, which can pay when it lowers the AMT. With that fixed, one household owed $2,070 less. Both mistakes showed up because two independent tools agreed with each other and not with us.

4. A search found the loopholes tax advisers already use

With a model that matches the reference software, we used it as we had used the retirement rules: as the oracle for a search that knows no tax planning. The first search tried ordinary choices for each of the 5,000 households, 195,787 returns in all:

  • file separately, and which spouse holds which investments, pays which bills and claims which children;
  • contribute to an IRA;
  • earn a little less;
  • realize more or less gain.

The second search used a multi-year family model, which adds the kiddie tax, trust taxation, Roth conversions, required withdrawals, gifts and death. It tried about 30,000 plans for four families over 34 to 47 years. Everything large that the two searches found is already in the planning literature:

What the search foundBest caseAlready described by
A business owner files separately to get under the §199A threshold$6,317 a yearKitces[12]
The lower earner claims the children on a separate return$3,090 a yearpractitioner guides[13]
Realize less gain to stay under the EITC investment limit$6,798 for $5,000 deferredIRS Publication 596[11]
Itemize a smaller amount to cut the AMT$2,070 a yearForm 1040 instructions
Roth conversions in the gap years before Social Security+$0.84M over a lifetimeKitces
Pay your children wages, and open Roth IRAs for them+$0.46MKitces[14]
Convert so the heirs do not stack ten-year withdrawals+$0.43M–0.57MJournal of Accountancy[15]

As with the backdoor Roth, none of these was described to the search. It found them because the rules, written down plainly, permit them.

5. Novel loopholes we found

Three results did not turn up in practitioner sources, IRS guidance or tax-software forums.

Filing separately can cut tax on Social Security, even for a couple living together. The standard advice is that a couple living together should never file separately when one draws Social Security.[16] A separate filer who lived with their spouse gets no base amount at all. But taxable benefits are capped at the lesser of 85% of benefits or 85% of provisional income,[17],[18] and the search found couples for whom that cap makes separate returns cheaper. On a joint return the working spouse’s wage counts in provisional income, so a moderate wage already pushes the benefits to the 85% maximum. On a separate return the retiree’s benefits are measured against the retiree’s income alone. With $48,000 of benefits and a $60,000 wage, the couple owes $7,050 jointly and $5,568 separately, $1,482 less. A second reviewer recomputed it by hand and got the same answer. At a $100,000 wage the result flips, so the window is real but narrow.

Wages on one return, investments on the other. The 3.8% tax on investment income applies to the smaller of the investment income and the excess of income over $250,000 jointly, or $125,000 on a separate return.[19] On a joint return, wages use up that threshold first. On separate returns the investing spouse’s income excludes the other’s wages, and their gains start in their own 0% band. With about $200,000 of each, that saves $1,621. Every explainer gives the threshold. We found none that describes the split or where it pays.

Schedule 8812 pays more than the statute allows. This is a gap between the IRS form and the law, not a plan. The statute caps the refundable child credit per qualifying child, computed without the $500 credit for other dependents. The form caps the combined credit instead, so in the phase-out range, with no tax left to absorb it, it refunds the $500 credits in cash.[20],[21] Example: one child and one other dependent, $240,000 of income, no tax left. The statute gives $200, the form $700. Lean proves the form is never below the statute and agrees with it exactly when there are no other dependents.

6. Why one year of the tax code holds no big loopholes

The backdoor Roth is big because two provisions combine to remove an income limit entirely, and the money then compounds tax-free for decades. A single year of the individual income tax is full of cliffs and per-return thresholds, but each is bounded: the largest swing we found was a few thousand dollars. Over decades, the large gains come from moves that are already published. The one combination we could not find written up was paying the children in the same years as Roth conversions, which adds about 0.5%. Our guess is that anything Roth-sized and unpublished lives where value moves between entities and their owners: partnerships, S corporations and C corporations.

7. Most of this can now run automatically

“The long-term problem is how this kind of bug-hunting can be done routinely, e.g. as part of a test suite. Some approaches aren’t really automatable, because they require a lot of both human and AI agent work.”

What still needs a person is deciding what a finding means. Some cliffs are deliberate. Others are in the IRS’s forms, not in the law, whilst others come from the way the official text is compiled, yet:

  • The text checks are routine. A new release is one download and one command, which fails on any fault the last release did not have, and git blame names the Act responsible.
  • The model is a one-off cost. Once written and proved, it is a build: if a later change breaks a proved property, the build fails. When the law changes, only the changed provisions need rewriting.
  • The comparison is routine once the input mappings are right. Getting them right was the hard part, and the same comparison found every mapping error.

Limits

  • Coverage. The model covers the 2025 individual income tax for a household record. It leaves out the kiddie tax on the single-year return, 28% and §1250 gain, foreign income, passive activity rules, and most AMT preferences. The multi-year model holds 2025 law constant.
  • Who checked what. The drafting triage and the reviews were done by AI agents against the official text, and have not been checked by a lawyer or CPA.
  • Agreement is not truth. Where all four calculators agree they may share a misreading. The theorems and the IRS-example tests are the check on the model itself.

The code, the certificates, the comparison and the searches are in the lean-proofs folder of global-law.[3]

References

  2. Alan Yahya, ‘LEAN proof to search for US tax loopholes’ (Lexifina, 9 November 2026) <lexifina.com/blog/searching-the-tax-code-for-loopholes>

item.title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live (225 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2026-11-06-ui-updates-complete/, See on Hacker News

In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community, the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details.

We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI.

Context¶

With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security.

Digital attestations, introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations.

To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide.

Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take.

The New Security Tab¶

The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from.

Provenance States¶

PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states:

Full Provenance¶

This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types:

PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher:

SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions:

You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information.

No Provenance¶

"No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified.

When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release.

Provenance Warnings¶

Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow.

When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install.

Incomplete Provenance¶

This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token).

Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing.

Inconsistent Provenance¶

This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories.

Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers.

Change of Provenance¶

This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover.

If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned.

Loss of Provenance¶

This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them.

Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified.

To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation.

Redesigned Project Detail Page¶

To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated:

  • Provenance warnings now appear at the top of the page, alongside status banners for yanked releases, archived projects, and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined, only the quarantine banner is shown, as it takes precedence over all other warnings and banners.
  • When a release has full provenance or provenance warnings, its provenance state is displayed in the sidebar, linking through to the security tab for more information.
  • Metadata is now ordered by utility and labeled as "PyPI data" or "Data verified by PyPI", replacing the old design where data was grouped and ordered by verification status.

Release Files and Release History¶

The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon.

Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days.

The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release).

Getting Help¶

Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about:

  • Assessing source code security
  • Checking provenance (where a package came from)
  • Verifying package integrity
  • Protecting yourself from common security attacks
  • Reporting security issues

Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments¶

The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project.

This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative. We would like to thank Dustin Ingram, Zach Steindler, and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler, Jacob Coffee, and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design.

Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem.

item.title: Show HN: DeepSeek V3 in ~200 lines of pure Jax (209 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax, See on Hacker News

The architecture from the DeepSeek-V3 technical report in 190 lines of pure JAX, pretrained from scratch on a MacBook Air on public-domain detective fiction.

No Flax, no Equinox, no PyTorch. Params are plain dicts of arrays and every part of the model is a function you can read top to bottom in deepseek_v3.py.

Read the write-up: DeepSeek V3 in 190 lines of pure JAX, with diagrams, the code explained piece by piece, and the results.

What's in the 190 lines

Idea from the paper What it does Where
Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) Caches one small latent per token instead of full keys and values: 480 → 144 numbers per token per layer here mla, init_cache
Decoupled RoPE One rotary key shared by all heads, kept outside the compressed latent rope, apply_rope, mla
DeepSeekMoE 1 shared expert that always runs + 16 routed experts, top-4 per token route, moe
Auxiliary-loss-free balancing A per-expert bias nudges routing toward idle experts; it changes which experts are picked, not their weights update_bias, route
Sequence-wise balance loss The small complementary loss from the paper (α = 1e-4) seq_balance_loss
Multi-token prediction (MTP) An extra module also predicts the token after next, weighted λ = 0.3 in the loss forward, loss_fn
Training and generation bf16 compute on f32 master weights; prefill + decode with the MLA cache make_train_step, generate

Results

One run of the default config on a MacBook Air M5 (24 GB):
Model 36.2M parameters, 13.6M active per token
Data 207 books, 21.7M training tokens (Hammett repeated 3×); validation is held-out crime fiction
Training 12,000 steps, ~98M tokens (~4.5 epochs), ~2.6 h
Speed ~10.7k tokens/s (median)
Validation loss 5.02 (step 250) → 3.51
Expert load, with bias 5.7–6.9% per expert (even is 6.25%), at step 2000
Expert load, without bias 0.09–18.6% per expert, at step 2000

With balancing on and off, validation loss at step 2000 was the same (3.921 vs 3.923). The bias evens out the experts without costing anything, which is the paper's claim.

Its own words, from the prompt "The fog came in off the":

The fog came in off the bay, and the great trees were spreading and the stars were shining.

This is an architecture demo, not a strong language model. See the write-up for what worked, what didn't, and what's missing.

Try the trained model

The v1.0 release has the exact checkpoint and data from the published run. After installing (step 1):

mkdir -p data runs/main
curl -L -o runs/main/ckpt.pkl      https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/ckpt.pkl          # 138 MB
curl -L -o data/tokenizer.json     https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/tokenizer.json
.venv/bin/python sample.py --prompt "The fog came in off the" --num 3

The checkpoint is a Python pickle, which can run code when loaded. Only load checkpoints from sources you trust.

Reproduce it

You need an Apple Silicon Mac, Python 3.12 and uv. The published run used 24 GB of memory. No Mac? See Running on CPU.

1. Install

git clone https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax.git && cd deepseek-v3-jax
uv venv -p 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt

Every version in requirements.txt is pinned. jax-metal 0.1.1 only works with jax==0.4.34, so don't upgrade JAX.

2. Check your setup

JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/pytest tests.py -q    # 39 passed
.venv/bin/python smoke_metal.py                   # optional: what jax-metal supports on your Mac

In smoke_metal.py, "grad through 2-axis contraction" fails on jax-metal 0.1.1. That's expected, and the model is written to avoid it.

3. Build the dataset

.venv/bin/python prepare_data.py

This downloads the 207 books in sources.txt (~120 MB, about 7 minutes), cleans them, trains an 8,192-token BPE tokenizer and writes data/train.bin, data/val.bin and data/tokenizer.json. It should print:

train: 211 docs, 83.4M chars, 21.69M tokens
val: 4 docs, 1.1M chars, 0.30M tokens

The published run's data had these hashes:

shasum -a 256 data/train.bin data/val.bin data/tokenizer.json
d37aca97e707bb81b6e4d266cc1adfd1f3e3556457c6eb724e495118a734e0bb  data/train.bin
b7ac285b115e6793b5d36aa5b4bc6e81a5fccfc7af0908a306d3828ebca9c31c  data/val.bin
c5a142b4006a967c880dda44ad792719d53c16d947da3b6c2332d6132d9967cc  data/tokenizer.json

You will most likely get different hashes. The Hammett books are pinned to exact Standard Ebooks commits and come out identical, but Project Gutenberg files can't be pinned, and Gutenberg has since re-issued 28 of the 203 books with small edits (mostly accents stripped, like "José" → "Jose"). The token counts come out the same, so training should behave the same.

To train on the exact same bytes, skip prepare_data.py and download the published data instead:

mkdir -p data
for f in train.bin val.bin tokenizer.json; do curl -L -o data/$f https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/$f; done
shasum -a 256 data/*.bin data/tokenizer.json    # should match the hashes above

4. Train

.venv/bin/python train.py                                         # the main run: 12k steps, ~2.6 h
.venv/bin/python train.py --steps 2000 --out runs/bias_on         # balancing ablation, with the bias
.venv/bin/python train.py --steps 2000 --out runs/bias_off --no-bias   # ...and without it

Each run writes metrics.jsonl (loss, validation loss, per-expert load, biases, tokens/s) and ckpt.pkl (saved at every evaluation) into its --out folder, which defaults to runs/main. Seeds are fixed, but GPU math on Metal isn't bit-for-bit deterministic, so expect your numbers to land close to the ones above rather than match them exactly.

5. Generate

.venv/bin/python sample.py --prompt "The fog came in off the" --num 3

Defaults: temperature 0.8, top-k 50, 300 new tokens per sample (--temp, --top-k, --n).

6. Make the figures

.venv/bin/python plots.py                    # needs runs/main, runs/bias_on, runs/bias_off
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/python charts.py # the rest of the write-up's charts

Both write into post/figures/.

To redraw the figures without training, download the logs from the release: metrics-main.jsonl, metrics-bias_on.jsonl and metrics-bias_off.jsonl go into runs/main/, runs/bias_on/ and runs/bias_off/ as metrics.jsonl. charts.py also needs the checkpoint and the data.

Running on CPU

Everything runs without jax-metal. It's much slower, so use the smaller config:

JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/python train.py --config small

--config small (4 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 128-token context) is meant for 8–16 GB Macs too. It has only been checked for a couple of steps, not trained to the end.

Files

File What it is
deepseek_v3.py The model: config, MLA, MoE, balancing, MTP, loss, train step, cached generation. The 190 lines.
train.py Training loop: AdamW with warmup and cosine decay, evaluation, checkpoints, logging
prepare_data.py, sources.txt Download, clean and tokenize the corpus
sample.py Text generation from a checkpoint
tests.py 39 tests: causal masking, cache vs full forward, routing, balancing, MTP targets, NaN handling, bf16 master weights, and more
smoke_metal.py Which JAX operations work on Apple's GPU
plots.py, charts.py The figures, all drawn from the logs, checkpoint and corpus
post/ Diagrams, figures and screenshots from the write-up

"190 lines" counts the non-blank, non-comment lines of deepseek_v3.py after its docstring:

tail -n +5 deepseek_v3.py | grep -cvE '^\s*(#|$)'    # 190

What's simplified

  • Dense MoE compute. Every expert runs on every token and the unpicked ones are zeroed. The routing math is exact, but there's no sparse dispatch or expert parallelism.
  • No weight absorption in MLA. The latent is decompressed explicitly, which is easier to read and slower at inference.
  • Not included: FP8 training, DualPipe, node-limited routing, YaRN context extension, and any post-training.
  • Scale. 36.2M parameters vs 671B, 6 layers vs 61, a 256-token context vs 128K.

Data and licensing

All training text is public domain in the United States: Dashiell Hammett's Red Harvest, The Dain Curse, The Maltese Falcon and Continental Op stories (CC0 editions from Standard Ebooks), plus about 200 detective and crime novels from Project Gutenberg. Every source is listed in sources.txt. Public-domain status outside the US may differ.

Reference

DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report, 2024.
