item.title: Demystifying phone unlocking tools: A technical overview (103 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://osservatorionessuno.org/blog/2026/05/demystifying-phone-unlocking-tools-a-technical-overview/, See on Hacker News

Introduction #

Commercial phone unlocking tools are not magic. They exploit the same classes of vulnerabilities that security researchers publish about at conferences and in academic papers. What makes them distinctive is not the novelty of the techniques, but the systematic commercialization of exploitation: acquiring or developing exploits for each hardware and software combination, and reaching a certain degree of stability, packaging them into automated workflows that require minimal operator expertise.

This post aims to demystify the technical foundations of these tools. The attack vectors available to a forensic examiner with physical access to a device are constrained by well-understood boundaries: the boot chain, the trusted execution environment, the secure element (when present), and the kernel’s peripheral driver stack. This post mostly details Android internals, however iOS equivalent concepts are technically similar.

Much of the background research referenced here comes from Quarkslab, whose extensive publications on TEEs, and Android’s data encryption architecture have been invaluable to understand these tools. Their work, alongside reporting from Amnesty International’s Security Lab and other NGOs, and analysis by the GrapheneOS project, provides the empirical basis for the claims made in this post.

Hardware security architecture #

Before examining attack vectors, it is necessary to understand the hardware security architecture of modern Android devices. The following sections describe the components that forensic tools must eventually hack or bypass.

The System-on-Chip: Normal World and Secure World #

Modern ARM-based mobile processors implement TrustZone, a hardware security extension that partitions the processor into two execution environments: the Normal World and the Secure World. The Normal World runs the Android operating system, user applications, and the Linux kernel. The Secure World runs a separate, minimal operating system, the Trusted OS, along with small, specialized applications known as Trusted Applications (TAs).

The two worlds share the same physical processor cores but are hardware-isolated: the Normal World cannot directly read or write Secure World memory. Communication between the two happens through a monitor, a piece of code running at the highest privilege level (EL3 on ARMv8), which handles context switches triggered by Secure Monitor Call (SMC) instructions. Each physical processor core effectively provides two virtual cores, with the Non-Secure bit in the Secure Configuration Register determining which world is active at any given time.

The Trusted OS hosts critical security services. Two are directly relevant to device unlocking:

  • Gatekeeper: responsible for verifying user credentials (PIN, password, pattern). It implements rate-limiting to throttle brute-force attempts and, upon successful authentication, issues a signed authentication token.
  • Keymaster: the key management service that stores and operates on cryptographic keys. Some keys are authentication-bound, meaning they can only be used after Gatekeeper has issued a valid token.

Different SoC vendors ship different TrustZone implementations. Google (and AOSP in general) uses TrustyOS; Qualcomm uses QSEE; Samsung uses TEEGRIS (on both Exynos and MediaTek SoCs in Samsung devices); Huawei uses TrustedCore; Trustonic’s Kinibi is also often found on MediaTek and Exynos SoCs. The security properties vary between implementations.

The Secure Element #

A Secure Element (SE) is a physically separate, tamper-resistant hardware chip that provides an additional layer of security beyond the TEE. Unlike the Secure World, which runs on the same SoC as the Normal World, a Secure Element is an independent processor with its own boot chain, its own firmware, and its own cryptographic key storage.

In the Android ecosystem, the Secure Element is exposed through the StrongBox API (introduced in Android 9). Google’s Pixel phones, starting with the Pixel 3, include the Titan M chip as their Secure Element, that was later upgraded with the Titan M2 from Pixel 6 onward. On Apple devices, the equivalent is the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP).

The Secure Element’s role in device encryption is to hold key-encryption keys and enforce rate-limiting for credential verification in hardware that the main SoC cannot tamper with, even if fully compromised. This is an important distinction: on a device without a Secure Element, compromising the TEE is sufficient to extract or bypass credential-derived keys. On a device with a Secure Element, the attacker must additionally compromise a separate, hardened chip.

Unfortunately, only flagship devices typically include a Secure Element. Most mid-range and budget devices rely solely on the TEE for credential protection. This architectural gap is the single most important factor determining the chances that a device has to resist forensic unlocking when powered off.

The boot chain #

The boot chain establishes a chain of trust from immutable hardware to the running operating system. Each stage verifies the integrity of the next before executing it.

The chain proceeds as follows:

  1. Boot ROM: the first code executed at power-on. It is burned into silicon at manufacture and is, in principle, immutable and unpatchable (with a few modern exceptions to deploy patches for vulnerabilities). The Boot ROM verifies and loads the next stage (the preloader or secondary bootloader). It forms the hardware root of trust.

  2. Preloader/Secondary Bootloader (BL2): loaded and verified by the Boot ROM. On MediaTek SoCs, this is often called the preloader. It initializes hardware, loads the Trusted OS into the Secure World, and loads the main bootloader into the Normal World.

  3. Trusted OS: loaded into the Secure World by the preloader. It hosts Gatekeeper, Keymaster, and other Trusted Applications. Its integrity is verified by the preloader as part of the secure boot chain.

  4. Bootloader (BL3): the Normal World bootloader (e.g., Little Kernel on MediaTek, ABL on Qualcomm). It enforces Android Verified Boot (AVB), anti-rollback protections, and device-state checks before loading the Android kernel.

  5. Android OS: the Linux kernel and userspace. Verified Boot (dm-verity) ensures the integrity of system partitions at runtime.

When a Secure Element is present, it runs its own independent boot chain in parallel: Boot ROM → Bootrom EXT → Bootloader → OS. The Secure Element’s boot chain is entirely separate from the SoC’s, providing the most isolation.

If any stage in the boot chain is compromised, all subsequent stages are untrustworthy. This is why Boot ROM vulnerabilities are so devastating: they are often unpatchable, they undermine everything built on top, and they affect every device using the vulnerable silicon for its entire hardware lifetime.

Android data encryption #

Understanding the attack vectors requires understanding what the attacker is ultimately trying to obtain: the decryption keys for the user’s data.

Full Disk Encryption vs. File-Based Encryption #

Android has used two encryption schemes over its history:

Full Disk Encryption (FDE) encrypts the entire data partition with a single key, derived from the user’s credentials. The key must be available before the OS can boot, so the user is prompted for their PIN or password at boot time. FDE was the default until Android 6 and has been deprecated since Android 13.

File-Based Encryption (FBE) encrypts individual files with different keys, allowing more granular access control. FBE has been the default since Android 7 and is required since Android 10. It divides storage into two classes:

  • Device Encrypted (DE) storage: available immediately after boot, before the user authenticates. Used for system-critical functionality (alarms, phone dialer, Direct Boot). The DE key is derived without user credentials.
  • Credential Encrypted (CE) storage: available only after the user authenticates for the first time after boot. This is where all user data resides—messages, photos, application data. The CE key is derived from the user’s credentials, stretched through scrypt, and protected by keys held in the TEE (and, when present, the Secure Element).

CE key derivation: The role of credentials #

Quarkslab’s Android Data Encryption in depth provides the most detailed public analysis of how the CE key is derived. The process, in simplified form, proceeds as follows:

  1. The user’s credentials (PIN, password, or pattern) are stretched using scrypt, a memory-hard key derivation function, with parameters and salt stored in DE-protected files under /data/system_de/<uid>/spblob. The scrypt step is intentionally slow: it introduces a negligible delay for a single authentication attempt but makes brute-forcing computationally expensive.

  2. The stretched credentials are combined with other material to form a password blob, which is sent to the Gatekeeper Trusted Application in the TEE. Gatekeeper verifies the blob against a stored password handle using an HMAC with an internal key. If verification succeeds, Gatekeeper issues a signed authentication token.

  3. The authentication token is presented to Keymaster, which uses it to unlock an authentication-bound key. This key is used to perform the first decryption of the Synthetic Password, an intermediate secret stored in encrypted form on the filesystem.

  4. The Synthetic Password is decrypted a second time using a key derived from the user’s credentials (the applicationId). This second decryption uses AES-GCM, which provides authenticated encryption: if the wrong credentials are supplied, the GCM tag will not match and decryption will fail. This is the cryptographic check that ultimately binds the CE key to the correct credentials.

  5. From the Synthetic Password, the system derives the CE file encryption keys used by the Linux kernel’s fscrypt subsystem to decrypt individual files.

The critical observation is that user credentials are cryptographically embedded in the key derivation chain. There is no way to bypass them purely through software attacks: an attacker who compromises the TEE can bypass the authentication token check, but they still need to brute-force the credentials through scrypt to derive the correct key material.

Key derivation with a Secure Element (Weaver) #

On devices with a Secure Element, the key derivation process includes an additional step. Instead of relying solely on Gatekeeper in the TEE, the system uses Weaver, a service running on the Secure Element. Weaver stores a secret value that is released only upon correct credential verification and enforces its own independent rate-limiting.

This means that even if an attacker fully compromises the TEE, or other Trusted Applications as shown by Synacktiv’s Kinibi TEE blogpost, they cannot extract the Weaver secret or bypass its throttling, if implemented properly. Brute-forcing must proceed online, at the rate the Secure Element permits, which, for a device like the Pixel with Titan M, means exponential backoff.

Attack vectors #

With the architecture established, we can now map the specific attack surfaces that forensic tools exploit. These fall into two main categories, corresponding to teo device states: powered off or powered on but never unlocked (BFU), and powered on and previously unlocked (AFU).

BFU attacks on devices without a Secure Element #

The most complete form of BFU attack targets the boot chain itself. If an attacker can compromise the Boot ROM or the preloader, they can break the entire chain of trust, including the TEE.

The attack proceeds as follows:

  1. Boot ROM exploitation: the attacker connects to the device via USB and exploits a vulnerability in the Boot ROM (or uses a vendor-specific download/recovery mode, such as MediaTek’s Download Mode or Qualcomm’s EDL mode) to gain code execution before the bootloader runs.

  2. Boot chain patching: with Boot ROM-level access, the attacker patches or replaces the preloader to disable secure boot verification of subsequent stages. This allows loading a modified Trusted OS and modified Trusted Applications.

  3. TEE patching: the attacker replaces or patches Gatekeeper to accept any credentials and issue valid authentication tokens regardless of input. They also patch or extract keys from Keymaster. As Quarkslab demonstrated in their proof-of-concept on Samsung A22 devices (MT6769V and MT6833V SoCs), this involved patching Samsung’s TEEGRIS operating system: first disabling verification of the root filesystem, then disabling TA signature verification, and finally patching Gatekeeper’s credential comparison to always succeed.

  4. Key material extraction: with a rooted Android system and a compromised TEE, the attacker extracts the encrypted Synthetic Password and the intermediate decryption result from Keymaster.

  5. Offline brute force: the attacker now has all the material needed for offline brute-forcing. The brute-force loop is:

    • Generate a candidate password
    • Stretch it through scrypt with the stored parameters
    • Derive the applicationId
    • Attempt AES-GCM decryption of the Synthetic Password
    • If the GCM tag matches, the correct credentials have been found

Because this brute-force runs entirely offline, on the attacker’s hardware, it is bounded only by computational resources and password complexity. A numeric PIN of six digits or fewer is trivially recoverable. Even longer numeric PINs fall quickly on dedicated hardware. Only a strong alphanumeric and symbols password provides meaningful resistance.

MediaTek devices are particularly vulnerable to this attack. Multiple MediaTek SoCs contain Boot ROM vulnerabilities that are publicly known and exploited by open-source tools such as MTKClient. Because Boot ROM code is immutable, these vulnerabilities cannot be patched: every device using the affected silicon is permanently compromised, regardless of Android version or security patch level. Quarkslab’s proof-of-concept targeted exactly this class of device, demonstrating the full chain from Boot ROM exploit to CE key recovery.

BFU attacks on devices with a Secure Element #

When a Secure Element is present, the attack chain is fundamentally harder. Even if the attacker achieves everything described above, they still cannot extract the Weaver secret from the Secure Element, under normal circumstances. Chances of a Secure Element exploit are pretty low, especially as being distributed as part of a widely available forensics commercial suite.

As anticipated, the Secure Element runs its own independent boot chain on physically separate silicon. Its keys cannot be extracted by the main SoC, and its rate-limiting logic is enforced in hardware that the attacker does not control.

The result is that brute-force can often only proceed online: each attempt must query the Secure Element, which enforces some kind of backoff. This slows down the attack significantly. A ten-digit PIN that falls in seconds to offline brute-force may take a long time against a properly implemented Secure Element. An alphanumeric password becomes likely unbreakable.

This is why, according to Cellebrite’s own February 2025 support matrix, brute-force capabilities are generally not available for Pixel devices with Titan M. The Secure Element is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

That said, the Secure Element is not immune to vulnerabilities. Quarkslab demonstrated code execution on the Titan M chip through CVE-2022-20233, a single-byte out-of-bounds write in the Keymaster task that could be exploited to hijack execution flow. This vulnerability has since been patched, but it demonstrates that Secure Elements, while vastly more resistant than TEE-only configurations, can still have issues. Google is offering up to $1,500,000 for a zero-click vulnerabilities on the Pixel Titan M2.

AFU attacks: The lock screen is just UI #

After the first unlock, the threat model fully changes. In AFU state, the CE decryption keys are loaded in memory and remain there. The lock screen is no longer a cryptographic barrier, it is just a user interface element, a screen overlay that prevents interaction but does not re-encrypt data.

This means that an AFU attacker does not need to brute-force credentials at all. They need to achieve code execution in the kernel or a privileged process, at which point they have direct access to the decrypted filesystem. The lock screen is bypassed, and no encryption needs to be broken.

The primary attack surface in AFU state is the USB interface. When a device is locked but in AFU state, the USB controller remains active and exposes the device’s kernel to a substantial attack surface.

As the diagram illustrates, a peripheral emulator connected to a locked device’s USB port can interact with the kernel through approximately 200 reachable drivers, including MTP (Media Transfer Protocol), MSC (Mass Storage Class), HID (Human Interface Device), Audio, and CVC (Communication Voice Class) subsystems. Each of these drivers is a potential attack surface for memory corruption vulnerabilities.

The exploit used by Cellebrite against a Serbian activist’s device in December 2024, as documented by Amnesty International, attempted to use at least three Linux kernel USB driver vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2024-53104: a vulnerability in the USB Video Class (UVC) driver.
  • CVE-2024-53197: an out-of-bounds write in the ALSA USB-audio driver, triggered when a malicious USB device provides a bNumConfigurations value exceeding allocated memory. This vulnerability affects legacy code present since Linux kernel 2.6.26 (2008) and was confirmed by CISA to be actively exploited in the wild.
  • CVE-2024-50302: a memory leak in the HID subsystem that exposes uninitialized kernel memory, including encryption keys and authentication tokens, when processing crafted USB HID reports.

The Cellebrite Turbo Link device, a specialized hardware adapter that connects between the forensic workstation and the target device, likely functions as a peripheral emulator capable of presenting itself as multiple USB device types in rapid succession, probing for each vulnerability to achieve kernel-level code execution.

Many of these USB drivers are loaded by default and remain reachable even when the device is locked. The kernel does not distinguish between a legitimate USB accessory and a malicious peripheral emulator, thus this is the main weakness that AFU exploitation often relies upon.

AFU attacks on locked devices in practice #

Once the attacker achieves kernel code execution through USB driver exploitation, the lock screen is irrelevant. The attacker can:

  • Directly read the decrypted filesystem, since CE keys are already in memory
  • Perform a Full File System (FFS) extraction of all user data
  • Access application data, messages, photos, credentials, and metadata
  • Potentially install persistent backdoors

As we already knew, a device in AFU state is fundamentally less secure than a device in BFU state, regardless of the strength of the user’s password or the presence of a Secure Element. The Secure Element protects credential-derived keys at boot; it does not protect already-decrypted data in memory after the first unlock.

This is confirmed by Cellebrite’s February 2025 support matrix, which shows AFU extraction capabilities even for devices (including recent Pixels with stock Android) that resist BFU attacks. Notably, according to the same documentation, GrapheneOS on Pixel devices resists AFU extraction, probably thanks to the attack surface reduction and the USB restrictions that are implemented beyond stock Android.

A note on iOS: checkm8 and USB Restricted Mode #

Apple devices face analogous attack surfaces. The checkm8 exploit, publicly released in 2019, targets an unpatchable Boot ROM vulnerability present in all Apple devices from the iPhone 4S through the iPhone X (A5 through A11 SoCs). Like MediaTek Boot ROM vulnerabilities, checkm8 cannot be fixed through software updates: every affected device is permanently exploitable.

For newer Apple devices, AFU attacks rely on USB-based exploitation. Apple introduced USB Restricted Mode in iOS 11.4.1 to mitigate this: if the device has been locked for more than one hour, the Lightning or USB-C port is restricted to charging only, disabling data connections that forensic tools require.

However, Quarkslab’s analysis of CVE-2025-24200 (reported by CitizenLab) revealed that USB Restricted Mode was bypassable. The vulnerability, reported by Citizen Lab and patched in iOS 18.3.1, allowed a physical attacker to re-enable USB data connections on a locked device by exploiting a flaw in the Accessibility framework. The profiled daemon, which handles device management settings, failed to check whether the device was locked before processing requests to disable USB Restricted Mode. In other words, the USB port was only soft-disabled: something as simple as a logic bug in the policy enforcement allowed it to be re-enabled.

Forensic vendors have already started producing countermeasures to Apple’s inactivity reboot. Cellebrite’s Spring 2026 release for Inseyets advertises a “Safeguard Mode” that “mitigates the impact of iOS inactivity reboot timers by preserving access to a device” — in practice, preventing the device from returning to BFU state once they have AFU access. Magnet Forensics ships a hardware product called GrayKey Preserve which similarly aims to suppress the auto-reboot, network wipes and remote wipes on captured devices. These tools likely ship the same AFU exploits in a different, locked-down chassis that performs only preservation rather than extraction, which is also why they can move faster than the full extraction suites.

Defensive implications #

The attack vectors described above lead to a clear set of defensive priorities.

BFU is your best defense #

The most impactful single action when facing potential device seizure is to power the device off. This returns it to BFU state, where:

  • CE storage is encrypted and keys are not in memory
  • USB driver exploitation cannot yield decrypted data
  • The attacker must compromise the boot chain and brute-force credentials
  • On devices with a Secure Element, brute-force is rate-limited by hardware

Enable Lockdown Mode on iOS #

iOS users should enable Lockdown Mode. It hardens the device against exploitation across messaging, web, and attachments, and there is public-record evidence of it stopping at least one extraction attempt: an FBI CART court filing on an iPhone 13 explicitly states that “Because the iPhone was in Lockdown mode, CART could not extract that device”. The mechanism is not officially documented, but it is consistent with what Lockdown Mode is known to do: shrink the reachable attack surface, restrict USB more aggressively, and block the configuration-profile and MDM enrollment that forensic and “jailbreak” tools have historically abused to sideload unverified components.

Auto-reboot: returning to BFU automatically #

If a device cannot be manually powered off, an automatic reboot mechanism provides the next best defense. After a configurable period without user authentication, the device reboots, returning to BFU state and purging decryption keys from memory.

GrapheneOS has implemented this feature for years. Apple introduced it in iOS 18. Stock Android on Pixel devices gained a limited version in Android 15, but its implementation remains less configurable and less aggressive than GrapheneOS’s. The feature is the most useful if the timeout is short (2-4 hours) and loses its value when its multiple days, as Google enforces likely as a result of negotiation with law enforcement. GrapheneOS in particular allows the timeout to be configured very low, precisely because the team has long considered the risk of an exploit being produced to inhibit the reboot itself.

USB port restriction #

Disabling USB data transfer when the device is locked directly eliminates the AFU attack surface described above. Android 15 introduces USB restriction options; iOS has had USB Restricted Mode since version 11. GrapheneOS provides more trustworthy and configurable USB restriction.

Password strength #

The brute-force analysis makes the case for strong passwords unambiguous:

  • A 4-digit PIN: trivially crackable offline, and crackable even online within hours to days
  • A 6-digit PIN: trivially crackable offline; crackable online within days to weeks depending on rate-limiting implementation
  • A pattern: equivalent to or weaker than a short PIN in entropy
  • An alphanumeric password of 10+ characters with mixed case and symbols: computationally unlikely to brute-force offline through scrypt; almost impossible to brute-force online against a Secure Element

The password is only required at boot. Biometric authentication (fingerprint, face recognition) handles daily unlocking, unless the user is in a jurisdiction where physical coercion is likely, whether lawfully or not. The marginal inconvenience of entering a strong password once after each reboot is minimal compared to the protection it provides.

Device choice #

According to Cellebrite’s own February 2025 documentation:

  • MediaTek-based devices: effectively no mitigation possible against BFU attacks due to unpatchable Boot ROM vulnerabilities.
  • Most non-Pixel, non-Samsung Android devices: considered unlockable, with few exceptions, due to a combination of delayed security updates, weak TEE implementations, and absent Secure Elements.
  • Samsung devices (Exynos): partial protection, varying by model and patch level.
  • Google Pixel with stock Android: resistant to BFU attacks on recent models, but AFU file system extraction is possible.
  • Google Pixel with GrapheneOS: resistant to both BFU and AFU attacks on recent models (6a and newer). This is the strongest protection available on any Android device.

A subsequent Cellebrite matrix leaked in October 2025 suggests Cellebrite has since also lost Full File System extraction support against unlocked GrapheneOS devices.

It is worth noting that alternative Android distributions such as LineageOS or CalyxOS, while valuable for other reasons, do not meaningfully change the forensic unlocking picture from the stock or vendor ROM.

Application-level encryption #

Applications that implement their own encryption layer with a separate password can provide defense-in-depth against full device compromise. Password managers’ master password vaults are a good example: even if the entire device filesystem is extracted, the vault remains encrypted under a key that the forensic tool has not obtained.

However, the effectiveness of application-level protection depends on several factors: whether the app actually implements its own encryption independently from the OS credential protection, whether decryption keys remain in memory after first unlock (making them vulnerable to AFU extraction), whether the app relies on the system biometric authentication (which, without a Secure Element, is broken along with the rest of the OS key hierarchy), and whether notifications or message previews are cached in plaintext outside the app’s encrypted storage.

Conclusion #

The way these tools operate is not magic nor secret. The more we collect samples, reverse engineer and read promotional and support material, the better we understand capabilities and defenses.

As we said many times these tools simply shouldn’t commercially exist. The companies that build these tools are active participants in the zero-day vulnerability trade, stockpiling security flaws that weaken every device, for every user, everywhere. The technical defenses described here are effective but place the burden on individuals and communities.

Update (20 May 2026): following feedback from Final of the GrapheneOS Foundation, this post was updated with information about iOS Lockdown Mode, forensic-vendor countermeasures to iOS inactivity reboot (Cellebrite Safeguard Mode and Magnet GrayKey Preserve), GrapheneOS’s auto-reboot design rationale, and the October 2025 Cellebrite matrix leak.

item.title: Serving GLM-5.3 at 607.8 tok/s across two Nvidia DGX stations with vLLM (133 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/when-one-gpu-isnt-enough-serving-glm-5-3-across-two-nvidia-dgx-stations-with-vllm/, See on Hacker News

Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs. 

The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.

Before starting, connect the two Stations with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook.

This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.

Prerequisites

  • Two GB300 DGX Stations running Linux, connected and validated with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook, including its GPU-memory RDMA test on both rails.
  • SSH and sudo access on both Stations with the same Linux username. Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit come preinstalled with the DGX Station software stack. Allow outbound access to the container registry, Hugging Face, and package repositories.
  • At least 464 GB of free disk space on each Station for its copy of the checkpoint, plus room for the vLLM container image and temporary files.
  • Acceptance of the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and the original GLM-5.3 license terms, listed on the model card. SPEED-Bench is governed by the NVIDIA Evaluation Dataset License Agreement.
  • A Hugging Face account and read access token, with access to the gated cais/hle dataset: sign in, open its page, and select Agree and access repository. Step 5 downloads SPEED-Bench prompts from this dataset.

The companion video follows the same workflow.

Step 1. Prepare the two Stations

This tutorial uses a separate computer, such as your laptop, to manage both Stations. Start by opening an SSH session to each Station from that computer. Alternatively, work from a local terminal on each Station. Run every command in this step on both Stations unless it starts with “On A.”

The two Stations run the same container and checkpoint in different roles: Station A (rank 0) hosts the API, and Station B (rank 1) runs only a worker, with no API server.

First, check Docker access and collect the network values you’ll use later:

docker version
ibdev2netdev
ip -br addr

The ibdev2netdev output lists the two direct rails, cx8r0 and cx8r1. Pick one for serving traffic, for example cx8r1, and note two things for it on each Station:

  • Its RDMA device, on the ibdev2netdev line that ends with the rail’s name. In mlx5_1 port 1 ==> cx8r1 (Up), the device is mlx5_1.
  • Its IPv4 address, on the ip -br addr line that starts with the rail’s name. In cx8r1 UP 192.168.101.1/24, the address is 192.168.101.1.

The rail name and device are the same on both Stations; only the IPv4 address differs.

Next, create ~/glm53.env on each Station. This file stores the values that later commands use:

nano ~/glm53.env

Paste the following block and replace each <...> placeholder, keeping the quotes, with the values you noted.

RANK="<NODE_RANK>"                    # RANK="0" on Station A, RANK="1" on Station B 
HEAD_IP="<STATION_A_IPV4_ADDRESS>"    # IPv4 address you noted on Station A; same in both files
WORKER_IP="<STATION_B_IPV4_ADDRESS>"  # IPv4 address you noted on Station B; same in both files
RAIL_IFACE="<RAIL_NAME>"              # Rail you picked, for example cx8r1; same in both files
RAIL_HCA="<RDMA_DEVICE>"              # RDMA device you noted, for example mlx5_1; same in both files

IMG=vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0-aarch64
IMG+=@sha256:4864d46625cbc3307623e29ac742030655e27249feba7b97ec925ce4cc4dfb56
MODEL_REPO=nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4
MODEL_REV=e3b8f9f2fad29727dfa95e766c5cac18ea1414bf
MODEL_HOST="$HOME/models/GLM-5.3-NVFP4"
CONTAINER=glm53-full
PORT=8000

if [ "$RANK" = 0 ]; then
  NODE_IP=$HEAD_IP; PEER_IP=$WORKER_IP
else
  NODE_IP=$WORKER_IP; PEER_IP=$HEAD_IP
fi

GPU_UUID=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=uuid,name --format=csv,noheader |
  awk -F, '$2 ~ /GB300/ {gsub(/ /,"",$1); print $1; exit}')

For example, with the default addresses on cx8r1, Station A’s file starts like this. Station B’s file is identical except for RANK="1":

RANK="0"
HEAD_IP="192.168.101.1"
WORKER_IP="192.168.101.2"
RAIL_IFACE="cx8r1"
RAIL_HCA="mlx5_1"

MODEL_HOST is built from your home directory, and Step 2 copies the checkpoint over SSH to the same path on Station B.

On both Stations, load the values and check storage, connectivity, and baseline memory:

source ~/glm53.env
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST" && df -h "$MODEL_HOST"
ethtool "$RAIL_IFACE"
ip link show dev "$RAIL_IFACE"
ping -I "$RAIL_IFACE" -M do -s 8972 -c 3 "$PEER_IP"
timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value
nvidia-smi

These checks catch cabling and addressing mistakes before they surface as NCCL timeouts. Expect a 400000Mb/s link, MTU 9000, successful jumbo-frame pings, and synchronized time. nvidia-smi should show no compute processes on the GB300. On a Station with a display GPU, Xorg can appear on both GPUs with a few MiB.

Step 2 copies the checkpoint from A to B over SSH, so A needs passwordless access to B. On A, create a key without a passphrase (see SSH keys for details), copy its public key to B after checking B’s host fingerprint, and confirm the login: 

ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id "$WORKER_IP"
ssh -o BatchMode=yes "$WORKER_IP" hostname

Step 2. Download and copy the model

Tensor parallelism requires both ranks to run the same software against the same weights. Start by pulling the pinned image on both Stations:

docker pull "$IMG" &&
docker image inspect "$IMG" --format '{{.Architecture}} {{.RepoDigests}}'

The pull can take several minutes. Matching arm64 digests mean both ranks run identical software.

On A, download the pinned checkpoint. At about 464 GB, it takes roughly an hour at 1 Gb/s, or about six minutes at 10 Gb/s:

mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST"
docker run --rm --network host -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model" \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc \
  "exec hf download '$MODEL_REPO' --revision '$MODEL_REV' --local-dir /model"

When hf download prints Downloaded, copy the files to B. On A:

ssh "$WORKER_IP" "mkdir -p '$MODEL_HOST'" &&
rsync -aH --info=progress2 --exclude '.cache/' \
  "$MODEL_HOST/" "$WORKER_IP:$MODEL_HOST/"

Each disk keeps the full checkpoint; vLLM partitions the weights across the GPUs at load time, with no further quantization.

On A, compare both copies (the check reads B’s file list over SSH), then validate the checkpoint:

(
  set -euo pipefail
  L=$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -path '*/.cache' -prune -o \
    -type f -printf '%P %s\n' | LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum)
  R=$(ssh "$WORKER_IP" "set -o pipefail; find '$MODEL_HOST' \
    -path '*/.cache' -prune -o -type f -printf '%P %s\\n' | \
    LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum")
  test "$L" = "$R"
  test "$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -maxdepth 1 \
    -name 'model-*-of-00050.safetensors' | wc -l)" = 50
  python3 -c "import json; c=json.load(open('$MODEL_HOST/config.json')); \
assert c['architectures']==['GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM']; \
assert c['quantization_config']['quant_algo']=='MIXED_PRECISION'"
  echo MODEL_READY
)

MODEL_READY means both Stations hold the same file names and sizes in the expected layout. MIXED_PRECISION is expected: NVFP4 quantization targets MoE-block linear weights and activations, not every tensor.

Step 3. Launch the distributed service

This step turns two machines into one service: the same launch script runs on both Stations, reads ~/glm53.env, and starts one vLLM rank on each. Two settings matter most if you adapt it: --max-model-len 98304, the context ceiling in tokens, which covers input plus output, and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93, which gives vLLM 93% of GPU memory. If you change other flags, change one at a time and test again.

For the latest recommended configurations, see NVIDIA’s Local AI recipe repository.

On both Stations, create a file named ~/launch-glm53.sh:

nano ~/launch-glm53.sh

The script enables multi-token prediction (MTP), a form of speculative decoding: the model’s MTP layer drafts four tokens per step, and vLLM verifies them with the full model before accepting them, so each step can produce several tokens. The gain depends on how often drafts are accepted, which varies with the prompt.

FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage, leaving room for more tokens. Prefix caching is enabled to avoid reprocessing prompt prefixes the server has already seen. Paste the script below; it checks your configuration, finds the RoCE GID index for the selected rail, and starts this Station’s vLLM rank in a container:

set -euo pipefail
source "$HOME/glm53.env"
case "$RANK" in 0|1) ;; *) echo "Invalid RANK" >&2; exit 1;; esac
test -n "$GPU_UUID"
test -f "$MODEL_HOST/config.json"
GID_INDEX=$(/usr/sbin/show_gids 2>/dev/null |
  awk -v d="$RAIL_HCA" -v ip="$NODE_IP" \
  '$1==d && $5==ip && $6=="v2" {g=$3} END {if(g!="") print g}')
test -n "$GID_INDEX"
HEADLESS=
if [ "$RANK" = 1 ]; then HEADLESS=--headless; fi
SPEC_CONFIG='{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}'
KERNEL_CONFIG='{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false,"moe_backend":"flashinfer_cutlass"}'
COMPILE_CONFIG='{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_DECODE_ONLY","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[5,10,20,40,80],"pass_config":{"fuse_allreduce_rms":false}}'

docker run -d --name "$CONTAINER" \
  --gpus device="$GPU_UUID" --network host --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  --device /dev/infiniband --cap-add IPC_LOCK \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model:ro" \
  -e RANK="$RANK" -e HEADLESS="$HEADLESS" \
  -e MASTER_ADDR="$HEAD_IP" -e MODEL_REPO="$MODEL_REPO" -e PORT="$PORT" \
  -e SPEC_CONFIG="$SPEC_CONFIG" -e KERNEL_CONFIG="$KERNEL_CONFIG" \
  -e COMPILE_CONFIG="$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
  -e NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1 -e NCCL_IB_HCA="$RAIL_HCA" \
  -e NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX="$GID_INDEX" \
  -e NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22 -e NCCL_IB_RETRY_CNT=7 \
  -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0 -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_SYMM_MEM=0 \
  -e NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" -e GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" \
  -e NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 -e NCCL_DEBUG=INFO -e NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET \
  -e NCCL_DEBUG_FILE='/tmp/nccl_%h_%p.log' -e VLLM_HOST_IP="$NODE_IP" \
  -e VLLM_EXECUTE_MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1800 \
  -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  -e VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 -e FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc '
    set -euo pipefail  
    # Use NCCL 2.30.7 from the image: older versions can deadlock
    # cross-node CUDA graph replays over RoCE (vLLM issue #52504).
    export VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH=$(python3 -c "import nvidia.nccl,os;
print(os.path.join(list(nvidia.nccl.__path__)[0], \"lib\", \"libnccl.so.2\"))")
    test -f "$VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH"
    EXTRA=()
    if [ -n "$HEADLESS" ]; then EXTRA+=("$HEADLESS"); fi
    exec vllm serve /model --served-model-name "$MODEL_REPO" \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port "$PORT" \
      --nnodes 2 --node-rank "$RANK" --master-addr "$MASTER_ADDR" \
      --master-port 29501 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
      --speculative-config "$SPEC_CONFIG" \
      --max-model-len 98304  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
      --block-size 128 --max-num-seqs 16 \
      --trust-remote-code --disable-custom-all-reduce \
      --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --enable-prefix-caching \
      --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 \
      --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
      --kernel-config "$KERNEL_CONFIG" --compilation-config "$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
      --distributed-timeout-seconds 1800 \
      --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm47 \
      "${EXTRA[@]}"
  '

Run the script on B first, then on A:

bash ~/launch-glm53.sh

Each command prints a container ID and returns immediately; the service is not ready yet. B’s worker waits for A to join, then each Station loads its share of the weights from local storage, prepares kernels, and captures CUDA graphs. This takes several minutes.

On A, follow the log to see when the service is ready (--since hides output from earlier runs):

docker logs --follow --since "$(docker inspect \
  --format '{{.State.StartedAt}}' "$CONTAINER")" "$CONTAINER"

When the log shows Application startup complete, press Ctrl+C to stop following it; the service keeps running.

At this point one model spans two machines. Neither GPU holds a complete copy, and neither can answer a request alone: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.

The remaining GPU memory holds the KV cache, which stores the context of in-flight requests. The startup log reports its capacity (GPU KV cache size). All requests in flight share it, so longer prompts or more users need more of it. If you run out, lower --max-model-len or send fewer requests at once.

Step 4. Verify serving and send a request

On A, check the API (127.0.0.1 is A itself):

docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 10 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health" >/dev/null && echo HEALTH_OK

HEALTH_OK proves that Station A answers. Next, on both Stations, check that the ranks communicate over GPU RDMA rather than falling back to TCP sockets. The check reads the NCCL logs that the launcher writes through NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, and the same block shows the loaded memory:

docker exec "$CONTAINER" bash -lc '
  set -euo pipefail
  files=(/tmp/nccl_*.log)
  test -e "${files[0]}"
  grep -hE "NET/IB.*GDRDMA|GPU Direct RDMA Enabled" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  grep -hF "$NCCL_IB_HCA" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  if grep -hE "NET/Socket|NCCL WARN|NCCL ERROR" "${files[@]}"; then
    exit 1
  fi
  echo RDMA_CHECK_OK
'
nvidia-smi

RDMA_CHECK_OK means the check passed with no warnings. In nvidia-smi, A shows the VLLM::Worker_TP0 process and B shows VLLM::Worker_TP1, one rank per GPU. The startup log reports about 218 GiB of weights per GPU, roughly half the checkpoint, which confirms that the model is split across the two GPUs.

On A, send a chat request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 120 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Quarterly units sold: Q1 = 120; Q2 = 180; Q3 = 150. Summarize the trend in one sentence and calculate the percentage change from Q1 to Q2."}],
    "temperature":0,"max_tokens":4096,
    "chat_template_kwargs":{"reasoning_effort":"low"}}' |
python3 -c 'import json,sys; c=json.load(sys.stdin)["choices"][0];
print(c["message"]["content"]); print("finish_reason:",c["finish_reason"])'

The response should look like this:

**Trend:** Units sold rose sharply in Q2 before partially declining in Q3, remaining above the Q1 level.

**Q1 → Q2 percentage change:** (180 - 120) / 120 × 100 = **50% increase**
finish_reason: stop

finish_reason: stop means the model finished its answer instead of hitting the token limit. The request sets reasoning_effort to low in chat_template_kwargs. GLM-5.3 also accepts high and max, which let it reason longer before answering, at the cost of latency. Because the launcher enables tool calling (--enable-auto-tool-choice), agent frameworks that use the OpenAI tools API can call the same endpoint.

Step 5. Concurrency and release resources

AIPerf, the NVIDIA benchmarking tool for inference endpoints, measures throughput and latency. Installing it inside the serving container can change vLLM’s dependencies, so on A, install it in its own virtual environment:

sudo apt update &&
sudo apt install -y python3.12-venv python3.12-dev build-essential &&
python3.12 -m venv "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0" &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" install 'aiperf==0.12.0' &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" check

The install should end with No broken requirements found.

AIPerf can send synthetic prompts or replay an existing dataset. This tutorial uses the 80 Coding conversations from SPEED-Bench, a set of real prompts built to evaluate speculative decoding, so MTP is measured on realistic text. SPEED-Bench’s preparation script fetches these prompts from several Hugging Face datasets, including the gated cais/hle: if you haven’t already, open its page and select Agree and access repository before you continue. Then, on A, log in to Hugging Face:

"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/hf" auth login

Next, download and prepare the dataset. See the official AIPerf guide for details:

SPEED_BENCH_DIR="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench"
mkdir -p "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"
curl -fLsS https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Skills/refs/heads/main/nemo_skills/dataset/speed-bench/prepare.py | \
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - --config qualitative --output_dir "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"

On A, check the dataset and service. Continue when the check prints BENCHMARK_READY:

(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  curl -fsS "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/health" >/dev/null
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - <<'PY_CHECK'
import json
from pathlib import Path
root = Path.home()
path = root / "datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
assert path.exists(), "Dataset missing: rerun the SPEED-Bench preparation"
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]
coding = [row for row in rows if row["category"] == "coding"]
assert len(coding) == 80, "Expected 80 Coding conversations"
assert sum(len(row["messages"]) for row in coding) == 89
assert all("FULL BENCHMARK DATA SHOULD BE FETCHED" not in message["content"]
           for row in coding for message in row["messages"])
print("BENCHMARK_READY: dataset has 80 Coding conversations, 89 turns in total.")

PY_CHECK
)

The full sweep covers concurrency 1, 8, 16, and 32. At each level, AIPerf sends 3×C warmup requests, then measures 10×C requests, where C is the concurrency. Some conversations are sent more than once at higher concurrency.

Benchmark requests use the model’s default reasoning effort (max) and an 8,192-token output cap; responses can finish before reaching it. Full sweeps can take several hours.

 A two-hour request timeout leaves room for long responses, --server-metrics collects server counters used to measure MTP acceptance, and --export-level raw keeps each response for inspection. 

For a quick test, run the block below on A with both containers running and no other API traffic. It tests C1 and C8 with prefix caching enabled, as in the reference measurements in Table 2, below.

(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  CODING_DATASET="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
  test -f "$CODING_DATASET"
 export CONCURRENCIES=${CONCURRENCIES:-"1 8"} # Quick run: C1 and C8.
  # Optional full benchmark: follow the reproduction instructions below.
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 16 -> export CONCURRENCIES="1 8 16"
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 32 -> export CONCURRENCIES=32

  RUN_DIR="$HOME/aiperf-results/blog-coding-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
  for C in $CONCURRENCIES;  do
    ART="$RUN_DIR/c$C"
    env -u HF_HUB_OFFLINE -u TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE \
      "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/aiperf" profile \
      -m "$MODEL_REPO" --url "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT" \
      --endpoint-type chat --streaming --tokenizer "$MODEL_HOST" \
      --custom-dataset-type speed_bench_coding --input-file "$CODING_DATASET" \
      --request-count "$((10 * C))" --warmup-request-count "$((3 * C))" \
      --osl 8192 \
      --use-server-token-count --concurrency "$C" --random-seed 42 \
      --request-timeout-seconds 7200 \
      --server-metrics "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/metrics" \
      --export-level raw --artifact-dir "$ART"
    printf "Results: %s\n" "$ART"
  done
  printf "Results directory: %s\n" "$RUN_DIR"
)

AIPerf saves metrics, raw responses, and logs in the results directory. Warmup requests are excluded from the reported metrics.

Optional: Reproduce Table 2. In ~/launch-glm53.sh from Step 3 on both Stations, keep --enable-prefix-caching and set --max-num-seqs to 16 or 32 for the corresponding group shown in the comments above. Before each group, stop and remove the current containers on A, then B (docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER", followed by docker rm "$CONTAINER"). Relaunch the updated script on B, then A with bash ~/launch-glm53.sh and wait for Application startup complete. On A, run the matching export CONCURRENCIES command from the comments, then rerun the AIPerf block.

To test without prefix caching, replace --enable-prefix-caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching in the Step 3 script on both Stations, then recreate the containers as above. Performance may differ from Table 2.

Figure 2 compares overall output throughput across measured requests with mean per-user throughput. Token counts include reasoning.

Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.

Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32. 

After the requests finish, stop the vLLM container on A, then on B:

docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER"
docker inspect --format \
  'Status={{.State.Status}} Running={{.State.Running}}' "$CONTAINER"
nvidia-smi

The status should read Status=exited Running=false, with no vLLM processes in nvidia-smi; the checkpoint, containers, and results stay on disk. To resume, run docker start "$CONTAINER" on B, then A, and repeat the Step 4 checks.

Troubleshoot common blockers

  • Missing variables or SSH failure: source ~/glm53.env after reconnecting; verify A-to-B key authentication and B’s fingerprint.
  • SPEED-Bench preparation fails with a gated-dataset error: sign in to Hugging Face with the same account, open the cais/hle page, select Agree and access repository, then rerun the preparation.
  • Startup or RDMA check failure: inspect docker logs "$CONTAINER" on both nodes; verify the checkpoint and the GID, and rerun the playbook’s validation (script 07).
  • CUDA out of memory: lower --max-model-len or concurrency, then retest.

Put the endpoint to work

You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory. That opens up work that’s hard to do on a hosted endpoint: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs.

Connect your own application using the vLLM serving documentation, then rerun AIPerf with your prompts to find the concurrency that fits your workload. A frontier-scale model is now ready to build on, right from your desk.

item.title: The Claude Delusion (146 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.netmeister.org/blog/claude-delusion.html, See on Hacker News

November 13th, 2026

Something weird happens to people who are successful. They start to think they're gods.

Actually accomplishing anything is obviously no strict pre-requisite of success. And maybe it's not so much "being successful", but rather "being rich". How do you become rich? Some people are just lucky. Lucky to have a physical talent, lucky to have parents able and willing to nurture your talent, and of course quite often lucky to have been at the right place at the right time1.

Being lucky doesn't mean they didn't also work hard. But even—especially!—the Paris Hiltons of the world, the children of Hollywood superstars, the crooks starting their corrupt empires with "a small loan" (or a share of an emerald mine) from their fathers—they all strongly believe that they deserve their success and then conclude that anybody not as successful only has themselves to blame.

This is especially the case for people in tech, where for years and years being good at programming has been equated with overall (and often: superior) intelligence2, and those illusory superiority effects then amplify rampant Dunning-Kruger to quickly turn "I am good at writing code, and with some luck, I managed to be successful" into a train of thought that goes more like "I am successful. Success is not random, so I must deserve my success. I appear to be a genius, I've mastered coding, anything else is trivial. Ergo, I am good at everything."

Bill Gates, MD / PhD Biology

Let's take Bill Gates as an example. Now, mind you, Bill Gates certainly has accomplished a lot, and his skillset and professional background includes without a doubt a lot of computer programming and various ruthless monopolistic business tactics. In a recent New York Times interview, he describes how he evaluated OpenAI's level of progress (emphasis mine):

And I was going down to see OpenAI on a regular basis to see the work they were doing, and I challenged them, saying: Hey, if you can read a biology textbook and pass the advanced placement exam — getting a perfect grade, which is a 5 — then you will have proven that you are reading. That is, encoding knowledge in an accessible form. And so it’s six months before the public release that Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever come to my house and demonstrate to me getting a 5 on the A.P. exam, even on questions that I had made up that it couldn't possibly have seen — very complex biology problems. It was nearly perfect. So that was shock No.1.

Now Bill Gates surely has shown an interest in biology and, through his work with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, has probably read a lot of articles and research in this field. But the hubris to think himself a subject matter expert able to make up advanced, novel questions in a scientific field outside his own and suitable to assess AI's true capabilities and then being "shocked" that it could answer these questions makes my point.

Although, what really cooks his noodle is the idea that AI can do what he used to do: write code.

And then late last year, when Anthropic's Claude coding models got super good, I could see that they are as good as I am — it’s significantly my most developed talent, because I was obsessed from age 13 to 24 as to whether I could write code as good or better than anyone. That’s another moment where I went: This is incredible. That the capability of doing long-running, complex tasks has now gotten to the point that they are superhuman at writing code and in finding flaws in code.

Take note of the emphasis I added: the very notion that something else could be "as good as I am" is, first of all, hard to believe and secondly necessarily means that it's "superhuman". That man is not lacking self-esteem, no sirree, Bob.

Likewise, this is also where many of the tech bros appear to be losing their minds, and this thinking ("Anything approaching my skill level is superhuman.") explains a lot about how we ended up with both stories of ultimate doom and human extinction as well as the utopian nirvana where AI solves all of mankind's problems (well, all of the billionaires' problems, which appear to largely converge on pesky mortality).

Revenge of the Nerds

For most tech nerds, being good at programming computers was a differentiating skill. It was weird, normies didn't understand it at all, you spoke your own language (languages!), you could make a computer do things. You understood how the internet works, and anything that's not working was clearly written by complete and utter morons, and you could easily write this yourself in an afternoon if you wanted to.

So now you've created a computer program that can do the same thing. Your mind boggles! And it speaks! It confirms you, it praises you, it tells you that you're brilliant—clearly evidence that it is infallible itself. But now imagine if it was better than you. What at first seems inconceivable then must strike fear and awe in your heart, for you have created a powerful monster with direction and purpose all its own. (And you sure have consumed enough pulpy science fiction to know that your creature is coming for you eventually.)

"Can you imagine a Beowulf cluster of these?" was an old Slashdot meme before memes were a thing. But the notion of having an army of minions to do your bidding has always appealed to the nerds looking to assert their superiority, and thus we arrived at "agents". "Swarms" of "autonomous" "agents".

This narrative of agency conveniently also relieves you of responsibility. You didn't fail to properly restrict a potentially malicious program you trained to hack other systems with persistence. No, the "agents" went "rogue". You have summoned powerful daemons indeed. Daemons that can produce code faster than you (gasp!), code you don't fully understand (although of course you could, you just don't want to, you don't have time, you have too much going on, what with your homegrown heavily customized harness). It becomes obvious quite quickly that this, then, must be SUPERINTELLIGENCE. Superintelligence that COULD KILL US ALL!

Power corrupts etc.

I picked on Bill Gates above to illustrate the overconfidence effect, but of course there is no shortage of much more exaggerated egos making bold statements outside of (or even within) their purported area of expertise, reflecting a complete and utter inability to relate to other people. To them, we're all just NPCs.

The more powerful people are, the less empathy they exhibit. This is neither news nor limited to tech; dog knows there are countless rich assholes outside of tech doing asshole things. But few outside the tech sector suffer the same level of delusion, of thinking themselves solely and uniquely qualified to decide mankind's future, to claim to have birthed a digital Prometheus, to boldly declare (and use as a perpetual shield) a literal Deus ex Machina to cure all diseases—if only they could find the time to prioritize that sort of work over, say, their military contracts.

Pretending to even remotely care about climate change3 while at the same time undoing "15 years' worth of greenhouse gas reductions" and then listing environmental concerns as a risk factor in your S1 is just the cherry on top.

If these are the new American Gods... well, je n'ai jamais eu besoin de cette hypothèse-là.

November 13th, 2026

Footnotes:

[1] The actual citation for "Bill Gates went to one of the only high schools in the world that had a computer" is "The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel; Malcolm Gladwell discusses this in Outliers as well. ↩

[2] The entire interview circus in the tech world revolved around this notion of exclusivity and brilliant jerks: "Google hires geniuses" was an oft-repeated mantra in Silicon Valley, so logically, if you were hired by Google, you were a genius. (Yes, all >180,000 of Google's employees.) This translates to the other big or exclusive companies, and explains why everybody leaving will always note that they were always surrounded by the most brilliant minds. It's Inverse Groucho Marx Bias. ↩

[3] And hey, we really don't need AI to "figure out how to combat climate change". We already know how to do it. We just have to actually show any willingness to stop it. Unfortunately, that's also exactly where these megalomaniacs get in the way. ↩

item.title: A visual explanation of reinforcement learning (135 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://aatishb.com/myriad/how-brains-learn/, See on Hacker News

How does your brain help you learn a new skill?

To try to answer this question, we’ll build a digital being with a simple brain, and watch it learn a new behavior.

In our previous article, we created a creature called a spark that could steer towards light. And we saw how small changes to its neural circuitry gave rise to very different behaviors.

Back then, we’d wired these circuits into the spark’s brain by hand. But now, we want it to learn the same behaviors by itself.

After all, you didn’t come into this world knowing how to walk, talk or read. While some of your abilities, such as breathing or swallowing, are wired by evolution, you gained others through an arduous process of trial and error.

We want our spark to do the same. To give you an intuition for this learning process, we’re going to hand over the controls to you. We’d like you to wire the spark’s brain.

You wire its brain

But first, we need to tell you what you’ll be wiring. The spark’s brain has just four neurons — two neurons serving as its eyes, and two neurons that wiggle its flippers.

There are straight connections between neurons on the same side of its body, crossed connections between neurons on opposite sides, and drive, which controls the spark’s speed when there’s no light.

So its brain wiring boils down to just three numbers — the strength of each kind of connection, and the drive.

Now let’s set this spark loose. Use the sliders below to wire its brain as it moves. We’ll keep score.

Your goal: Make the spark love the light by getting a score above 0.5.

Finding the right configuration takes a lot of trial and error. (If you get stuck, click the hint button above for a nudge in the right direction.)

Let’s visualize what you just did. To guide the spark to the light, you tweaked three numbers. We can represent these numbers as the three axes of a cube.

The payoff of this picture is that we can visualize your spark’s learning trajectory as a path within this cube.

Your learning path...

To guide the spark, you probably nudged a slider one way, saw whether this made things better or worse, and then used this feedback to decide your next move.

Let’s distill this into a learning algorithm — a step-by-step procedure by which the spark can rewire its brain through practice.

Here’s how it’ll work: The spark gets many tries to steer towards the light. Before every trial, its brain wiring will change a little at random, just like you wiggled the sliders to and fro.

If the trial goes better than previous ones, then the spark gets a reward and its wiring shifts in the direction of this random change. And if the trial goes worse, the spark gets a punishment, and its wiring shifts the other way.

This isn’t that different from how you learned how to walk or ride a bike. Falling down was your punishment, and the thrill of balancing was your reward.

Can this simple algorithm help the spark find the light?

A spark learns by itself

In the beginning, the spark is a novice, with a brain that’s wired together at random. Unsurprisingly, it doesn’t get very far.

The baby spark can spin in place, but it can’t yet move around. But it’s about to get better…

After 50 tries of this learning algorithm, our infant spark has taken its first steps. And while it won’t break any speed records, it’s now on the move…

After 250 tries, our juvenile spark has picked up speed. But it veers away from the light at the last moment.

After 500 tries, our adolescent spark boldly charges towards the light. But it hasn’t yet figured out how to slow down or stop.

After 2,000 tries, our spark is now an adult — an expert at seeking and following the light. It clings to the light and can turn on a dime. (Try moving the light to see the spark follow it.)

Like before, we can visualize this learning process as a path.

The spark’s learning path after 0 tries...

This isn’t a path through physical space. Instead, it’s a path through the space of possible brains. It shows how the spark’s brain changed as it learned.

Other novice sparks would start from different points, and they would each trace out their own learning trajectory.

Many sparks’ learning paths after 0 tries...

This tangled web illustrates the learning paths of hundreds of novice sparks, each starting with a differently wired brain. As if by magic, all of these threads converge to the point marked ♥︎.

The paths aren’t straight lines: Learning isn’t linear. There are setbacks, wrong turns and mistakes along the way. And it isn’t necessarily fast. Some of the learners took thousands of tries to reach their goal.

You’ll notice that the paths are all jittery. That’s because every step involves randomness. We can smooth out this jitter by averaging over many trajectories at every point, revealing a map of the flow of learning.

It’s worth taking a moment to appreciate how surprising this is — given enough tries, the same learning process turned every novice into an expert light seeker.

Of the myriad possible arrangements of this spark’s brain, only a tiny fraction generate the behavior that we want. There are far more ways to fail than to succeed.

And yet, you’ve just witnessed a small miracle. The spark navigated this labyrinth of dead ends and rewired its brain to find the light, guided by nothing but reward and punishment.

Learning new tricks

Learning doesn’t stop once you become an adult. We learn throughout our lives and adapt to changing circumstances.

Our sparks can do this too. For example, what if the light represents a harmful chemical or a dangerous predator instead of a food source?

The spark is now rewarded for avoiding the light rather than for seeking it, and this leads to new behaviors:

If the light is harmful, then LOVE becomes the worst strategy, and the sparks learn to FLEE (escape as fast as possible) or to FREEZE (play dead).

If instead the spark is rewarded for approaching the light with high speed, then it learns to charge towards the light, i.e. to FIGHT.

Much like a child learns from its environment, the spark can learn very different behaviors — fleeing, freezing, fighting or following the light — depending on how it’s rewarded.

You’ve now seen how a novice spark can rewire its brain and learn new behaviors through a process known as reinforcement learning.

Biological brains also learn through reinforcement. For example, baby songbirds learn to sing by babbling. They try out random variations of their song. If a variation gets closer to their memory of an adult’s song, they get a burst of dopamine (and if it gets further away, the dopamine dips). Guided by these rewards and punishments, they can recreate the song from memory, even with no teacher present!

Now, we do have to come clean about something. This spark’s brain had just four neurons and three numbers that determined how these neurons were connected. This simple structure allowed us to watch its brain learn in three dimensions.

Your brain has around 86 billion neurons and over a hundred trillion connections. The space of possible ways in which it could be wired is therefore unimaginably vast.

But while the details are much more complicated, the underlying idea is the same: Learning is how you navigate this vast internal space. And feedback is the compass that points the way.

Learn more

Thanks for reading chapter two of Myriad, a series exploring how minds emerge from matter. Myriad is a collaboration between Arkarup Banerjee, a neuroscientist who studies behavior, and Aatish Bhatia, a physicist turned science journalist.

How the spark moves

The sparks in this article are inspired by the work of the neuroscientist Valentino Braitenberg. We implemented their neural circuitry as follows:

vL=σ(ws bL+wc bR+d)vR=σ(wc bL+ws bR+d)\begin{aligned}v_L &= \sigma(\textcolor{#7ee081}{w_s}\, b_L + \textcolor{#c49bff}{w_c}\, b_R + \textcolor{#ff8fb8}{d})\\ v_R &= \sigma(\textcolor{#c49bff}{w_c}\, b_L + \textcolor{#7ee081}{w_s}\, b_R + \textcolor{#ff8fb8}{d})\end{aligned}

where vLv_L and vRv_R are the left and right flipper speeds, bLb_L and bRb_R are the brightness levels at the left and right eyes, ws\textcolor{#7ee081}{w_s} and wc\textcolor{#c49bff}{w_c} are the straight and crossed connection strengths between the eyes and the flippers, and d\textcolor{#ff8fb8}{d} is a drive that sets the spark’s speed when there is no light. σ(x)\sigma(x) is the ReLU function. The spark’s forward speed is the average of the two flipper speeds, and its turning speed is proportional to their difference.

How the spark learns

There are three parameters in our simplified setup: ws,\textcolor{#7ee081}{w_s}\textrm{,} wc\textcolor{#c49bff}{w_c} and d.\textcolor{#ff8fb8}{d}\textrm{.} The spark learns values for these parameters using a version of the REINFORCE algorithm published by Ronald Williams in 1992.

Each trial, the parameters were wiggled by a small random amount and the spark moved for 500 time steps, starting from a random point on the edge of the arena. Its reward was the average brightness along its path.

This reward was then compared to a running average of recent rewards. If the spark did better than usual, its parameters were nudged in the direction of this random change. If it did worse, its parameters were nudged in the opposite direction. The size of the nudge was proportional to how much better (or worse) it did:

ΔW(R‾)change=α(R‾)step sizeε(R‾)wiggle(R−R‾)(R‾)improvement\small \underset{\mathclap{\htmlClass{sans}{\text{change}}}}{\Delta W\vphantom{(\overline{R})}}\hspace{0.3em}=\hspace{0.5em}\underset{\mathclap{\htmlClass{sans}{\color{#66b3ff}\text{step size}}}}{\textcolor{#66b3ff}{\alpha}\vphantom{(\overline{R})}}\hspace{2.1em}\underset{\mathclap{\htmlClass{sans}{\color{#ff9b32}\text{wiggle}}}}{\textcolor{#ff9b32}{\varepsilon}\vphantom{(\overline{R})}}\hspace{1.2em}\underset{\mathclap{\htmlClass{sans}{\color{#ffc832}\text{improvement}}}}{\textcolor{#ffc832}{(R - \overline{R})}\vphantom{(\overline{R})}}

Here ΔW\Delta W is the change in the three parameters, α\textcolor{#66b3ff}{\alpha} is the learning rate, ε\textcolor{#ff9b32}{\varepsilon} is the random wiggle, and R−R‾\textcolor{#ffc832}{R - \overline{R}} is how much better or worse than usual the spark did. We repeated this thousands of times.

Williams’ original approach adds randomness to each neuron’s output. We add it to the weights and biases instead, an approach known as weight perturbation. A similar idea, called evolution strategies, was used by OpenAI in 2017 to teach AI models to play Atari video games.
